edges.basis: Psalm 2 and Matthew place son-language inside public claims about rule and response. Matthew adds visible transformation, cloud, named witnesses, and a command to listen.

edges.basis: Both scenes join mountain ascent, selected companions, six days, cloud, glory, and divine speech. Moses enters Sinai’s cloud; Matthew places Moses beside the transfigured Jesus inside another event.

edges.basis: Exodus and Matthew make a face visibly radiant around mountain revelation. Exodus explains Moses’ radiance through speaking with the LORD; Matthew describes Jesus being transfigured.
edges.label: Moses’ shining face and Jesus’ shining face

edges.basis: Deuteronomy commands Israel to listen to the prophet God will raise; Matthew’s voice commands the disciples to listen to Jesus. Matthew does not quote the full Deuteronomy passage or erase its original covenant setting.
edges.label: The promised prophet and “listen to him”

edges.basis: Malachi names Moses and Elijah; Matthew’s descent discussion returns to Elijah after both figures appear. Malachi’s oracle and Matthew’s explanation remain distinct claims about expectation and fulfillment.
edges.label: Moses remembered, Elijah promised, Elijah discussed

edges.basis: Matthew repeats beloved-Son and divine-pleasure language in two major events. The mountain adds transformed appearance, three disciples, Moses, Elijah, cloud, and “listen to him.”
edges.label: The voice at river and mountain

edges.basis: Matthew places the mountain after Peter’s confession, Jesus’ suffering prediction, discipleship language, and Kingdom sight. The sequence invites inquiry but does not state that the mountain exhausts the Kingdom promise.
edges.label: Confession, suffering, Kingdom, and the mountain

edges.basis: Mark places the transfiguration directly after the promise that some will see God’s Kingdom come with power. Mark preserves the sequence without giving a one-sentence identification of promise and event.
edges.label: Kingdom with power and Mark’s mountain

edges.basis: Luke places prayer, confession, suffering, future glory, and Kingdom sight before the prayer and glory of the mountain. The later scene develops the approach without reducing every prior saying to itself.
edges.label: Glory promised and glory seen

edges.basis: Both preserve six days, three disciples, transformation, Moses and Elijah, tents, cloud, voice, and Jesus alone. Matthew emphasizes shining face, bright cloud, prostration, and touch; Mark emphasizes dazzling clothes and Peter’s terror.
edges.label: Matthew and Mark on the mountain

edges.basis: Both preserve three disciples, changed appearance, Moses and Elijah, glory, tents, cloud, voice, and silence. Matthew says after six days; Luke says about eight, adds prayer, sleep, and the departure to be completed at Jerusalem.
edges.label: Matthew and Luke on the mountain

edges.basis: Both preserve transformation, white clothing, Moses and Elijah, fearful witnesses, cloud, voice, and silence. Luke adds prayer and the conversation’s subject; Mark states that Peter does not know what to say.
edges.label: Mark and Luke on the mountain

edges.basis: Matthew and Mark preserve the silence command, resurrection boundary, and Elijah question. Mark foregrounds questioning about rising; Matthew names the disciples’ conclusion about John the Baptizer.
edges.label: Two accounts of the descent

edges.basis: Matthew carries the same disciples from divine voice and fear into a father’s appeal and failed healing. The valley exposes little faith and another death prediction without undoing what was seen above.
edges.label: Glory above and failed healing below

edges.basis: Mark joins frightened witnesses, public dispute, a father’s mixed belief, private prayer instruction, and another passion prediction. The two scenes preserve different forms of fear, uncertainty, and failed understanding.
edges.label: Terror on the mountain and contested belief below

edges.basis: Luke moves from seen glory and the chosen Son to a father’s only child, healing, amazement, and concealed understanding. Public marvel does not produce understanding of the betrayal prediction.
edges.label: Glory, an only child, and a concealed saying

edges.basis: John and Matthew both join seen glory with unique Son-language. John does not name the mountain, so the relationship remains possible development rather than explicit event memory.
edges.label: Seen glory and narrated mountain glory

edges.basis: Paul explicitly reuses the Exodus facial-glory scene while contrasting ministries and speaking of transformation. Neither passage directly narrates the Gospel transfiguration.
edges.label: Moses’ face and Paul’s transformation argument

edges.basis: Matthew narrates the event; 2 Peter explicitly claims remembered sight and hearing on the holy mountain. The later memory selects majesty, honor, glory, voice, and prophetic confirmation rather than retelling every detail.
edges.label: The mountain scene and Peter’s eyewitness claim

event.centerRule: The Transfiguration remains the Event center. Related texts enter only when they materially prepare, locate, witness, develop, contrast, or remember the Event, and every Gospel witness keeps its own wording and sequence.

event.throughline: The trail moves from earlier mountain, glory, Moses, Elijah, son, servant, and listening language through the Synoptic approach, three mountain witnesses, descent, valley aftermath, and later memory.

topic.orientation: Enter the Transfiguration through each Synoptic witness, then follow the approach, changed appearance, cloud, voice, descent, valley aftermath, and later memory that Scripture places around it.
